title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Range Requests
summary: Defines range requests in HTTP/1.1 and the rules for building and combining responses to them. This lets a client ask for just part of a resource. It was later replaced by RFC 9110.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of downloading a whole movie, you can ask for just the middle part. This document explains how a browser asks for a piece of a file. It was later replaced.

questions: how do http range requests work
how to resume an interrupted http download
subtitle: Requesting and responding to partial content in HTTP/1.1.

tldr.problem: HTTP clients often want to resume interrupted downloads or request only a portion of a large file, but HTTP always returns the complete resource.
tldr.mechanism: Defines Range requests and partial responses: clients use the Range header to request byte ranges, servers respond with 206 Partial Content containing Content-Range headers, and multiple ranges can be sent as multipart/byteranges.
tldr.outcome: Enables efficient recovery from interrupted transfers and partial retrieval of large documents. It was replaced by RFC 9110.

today: RFC 9110 replaced this specification as part of the HTTP Semantics specification.

sections.title: Problem and Overview
sections.content:
HTTP clients often encounter interrupted transfers due to canceled requests or dropped connections. When a partial representation is already stored, it would be efficient to request only the remainder. Devices with limited storage might also benefit from requesting only a subset of a large file, such as a single page of a document or the metadata of an image.

Range requests are an optional HTTP feature designed for interoperability: recipients not implementing the feature can respond as if it is a normal GET request. Partial responses use a distinct 206 status code to avoid confusion with complete 200 responses in caching systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a download breaks halfway through. Instead of starting over, it is better to ask for just the missing part. Some devices have little space and want to download part of a file at a time, like one page of a big PDF.

sections.title: Range Units and Byte Ranges
sections.content:
A representation can be partitioned into subranges according to various structural units. The most common is the byte range, which partitions the data's octet sequence. A byte-range-spec has a first-byte-pos (inclusive byte offset starting at 0) and an optional last-byte-pos (inclusive). If last-byte-pos is absent or beyond the file length, the range extends to the end.

Clients can request the last N bytes using a suffix-byte-range-spec (e.g., bytes=-500). Multiple ranges can be requested in one Range header (e.g., bytes=0-499,9500-9999 for the first and last 500 bytes). The RFC also allows for future extensibility with other range units beyond bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask for bytes 0-499 (the first 500 bytes), or 9500- (from byte 9500 to the end), or -500 (the last 500 bytes). You can also ask for multiple separate parts in one request.

sections.title: Range Request Headers
sections.content:
The Range header field modifies GET request semantics to request only the specified subranges instead of the entire representation. Servers may ignore the Range header, but origin servers and caches should support byte ranges when possible. Servers MUST ignore Range headers with unrecognized range units or those on non-GET methods.

The If-Range header is a conditional precondition used with Range. If the If-Range validator (an entity-tag or HTTP date) matches the current representation, the server sends the requested ranges. If it does not match, the server ignores the Range header and sends the entire representation. This allows a client to efficiently handle a file that may have been modified since the partial copy was stored.
sections.plainLanguage: The Range header says what bytes you want. The If-Range header says "only send me the range if the file hasn't changed since I last saw it; otherwise send me the whole thing."

sections.title: 206 Partial Content Response
sections.content:
When a server successfully fulfills a range request, it sends a 206 Partial Content response. For a single-range request, the server MUST include a Content-Range header indicating the range (e.g., bytes 21010-47021/47022, where the first number is the range and the second is the total length) and the partial content as the payload.

For multiple-range requests, the server generates a multipart/byteranges payload with a boundary parameter. Each part has its own Content-Range header and optionally the original Content-Type. The server MAY coalesce overlapping ranges or ranges separated by small gaps if the overhead of multiple parts would be inefficient.

The server MUST include representation metadata headers (Date, Cache-Control, ETag, Expires, Content-Location, Vary) in the 206 response as they would appear in a 200 response.
sections.plainLanguage: For one range, the server sends status 206, tells you the bytes you are getting with a Content-Range header, and sends those bytes. For multiple ranges, it sends them as parts of a multipart message, each with its own Content-Range.

sections.title: Range Validation and Combining
sections.content:
A client that has received multiple partial responses to the same resource can combine them into a larger continuous range if they share the same strong validator (entity-tag or strong date). If the most recent response is a complete 200 OK, that response's header fields are used for the combined result. If the most recent is a 206 and any stored response is 200, the combined result uses the 200 response's headers.

The combined response body consists of the union of all partial content ranges. If the union covers the entire representation, the client treats the combined response as a complete 200 response with an appropriate Content-Length. Otherwise, the client processes it as a partial response with appropriate status codes reflecting whether it is a prefix, middle, or complete representation.
sections.plainLanguage: If you get part 1, then part 2, then part 3, and all came from the same unchanged file (same validator), you can glue them together. If together they make the whole file, great! If not, you know you still need the missing parts.

sections.title: Invalid and Unsatisfiable Ranges
sections.content:
A byte-range-spec is invalid if the last-byte-pos is present and less than the first-byte-pos. A byte-range-set is unsatisfiable if all ranges request positions beyond the current representation length. For invalid or unsatisfiable range requests, the server sends a 416 Range Not Satisfiable response with a Content-Range header in the format bytes */1234, indicating the complete length of the representation.

Servers should be cautious about processing Range headers with excessive numbers of overlapping or non-contiguous ranges, as these may indicate a broken client or a denial-of-service attack. Clients should list multiple ranges in ascending order and should not request ranges so fragmented that it would be less efficient than retrieving the entire representation.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask for bytes 500-100 (backwards), that is invalid. If you ask for bytes 0-1000000 and the file is only 100 bytes, it is unsatisfiable. The server responds with status 416 and tells you the actual file length so you can try again.
